nodes.name: Basis-function plant output model
nodes.statement: The dynamic relation between the plant inputs and each of the plant outputs $y_j(t),\, j=1,\hdots,n_y$, is given by: \beq \begin{aligned} y_j(t)&=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n_u}\sum\limits_{k=1}^{m}h_{ji}(k)\zeta\left(\mathcal{L}_k(a,q),u_i(t)\right)+d_j(t)= H_j^T\varphi(t)+d_j(t), \end{aligned} \eeq
nodes.statement_short: Each plant output is a finite basis-function expansion of the inputs plus an output disturbance.

nodes.name: Basis-function output operator $\zeta$
nodes.statement: the operator $\zeta\left(\mathcal{L}_k(a,q),u(t)\right)$ denotes the output of a linear system represented by the transfer function $\mathcal{L}_k(a,q)$ at the time step $t$, when the signal $u$ is applied as its input: \beq \zeta\left(\mathcal{L}_k(a,q),u(t)\right)\doteq \sum\limits_{l=1}^{\infty}\Psi_k(a,l)u(t-l), \eeq where $\Psi_k(a,l)$ are the impulse response coefficients of the basis function $\mathcal{L}_k(a,q)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\zeta(\mathcal{L}_k,u)$ is the convolution of the input with the impulse response of basis function $\mathcal{L}_k$.
nodes.genus: the output of a linear system represented by the transfer function $\mathcal{L}_k(a,q)$ at the time step $t$
differentia: when the signal $u$ is applied as its input

nodes.name: Regressor vector $\varphi(t)$ and modeling coefficient vectors $H_j$
nodes.statement: $\varphi(t)\doteq [\zeta\left(\mathcal{L}_1(a,q)u_1(t)\right), \hdots,\\\zeta\left(\mathcal{L}_m(a,q)u_1(t)\right),\hdots, \zeta\left(\mathcal{L}_1(a,q)u_{n_u}(t)\right), \hdots, \zeta\left(\mathcal{L}_m(a,q)u_{n_u}(t)\right)]^T$ is the regressor vector and each of the vectors $H_j\in \bR^{n_um},\, j=1,\hdots, n_y$ contains $n_ym$ modeling coefficients needed to describe the influence of all the control inputs on the plant output $j$: $H_j\doteq[h_{j1}(1), \hdots, h_{j1}(m), \hdots, h_{jn_u}(1), \hdots, h_{jn_u}(m)]^T$.
nodes.statement_short: The regressor stacks all basis-function outputs of all inputs; $H_j$ stacks the $n_um$ modeling coefficients of output $j$.

nodes.name: Matrix form of the plant output
nodes.statement: By defining the matrix $H\in \bR^{n_y\times n_um}$ as $H \doteq \left[H_1, \hdots, H_{n_y}\right]^T$, the dependence of the plant output on the regressor and the disturbance vectors can be written as: \beq y(t)=H\varphi(t)+d(t). \eeq

nodes.name: Remark on common $a$ and $m$ for all input-output pairs
nodes.statement: Note that the same value of the parameter $a$ and the number of modeling coefficients $m$ is assumed for all the input-output pairs, in order to simplify the notation. All the results can easily be extended to the case when different values for $a$ and $m$ are assumed for each input-output pair.

nodes.name: Noise-corrupted measured output
nodes.statement: The measured output available for feedback control is corrupted by noise. In particular, the vector of measured plant outputs is given as: \beq \tilde{y}(t)=y(t)+v(t), \eeq where $v(t)=[v_1(t),\hdots,v_{n_y}(t)]^T$ and $v_j(t),\, j=1,\hdots,n_y$ are the individual measurement noise terms that affect each of the measured plant outputs.

nodes.name: Assumption 1 (Prior assumption on disturbance and noise)
nodes.statement: (Prior assumption on disturbance and noise) $d$ and $v$ are bounded as: \beq \ba{lll} |d_j(t)|&\leq&\epsilon_{d_j}\\ |v_j(t)|&\leq&\epsilon_{v_j} \ea,\,\forall t\in\bZ,\,\forall j=1,\hdots,n_y, \eeq where $\epsilon_{d_j}$ and $\epsilon_{v_j}$ are positive scalars.
nodes.statement_short: Output disturbance and measurement noise are uniformly bounded componentwise by known positive scalars.

nodes.name: Assumption 2 (Prior assumption on the system)
nodes.statement: (Prior assumption on the system) The plant belongs to the following model set: $H\in \mathcal{F}(0)$, with \beq \mathcal{F}(0) \doteq \left\{H\in \bR^{n_y\times n_um}: A_{j}(0)H_j\leq b_{j}(0), j=1,\hdots, n_y \right\}, \eeq where the inequalities in \eqref{Eq:system_set} should be interpreted as element-wise inequalities and each matrix $A_{j}(0)\in \bR^{r_{j}(0)\times n_um}$ and vector $b_{j}(0) \in \bR^{r_{j}(0)}$ define a close and convex set, i.e. a polytope with $r_{j}(0)$ faces.
nodes.statement_short: The true coefficient matrix lies in a known initial polytopic model set $\mathcal{F}(0)$.

nodes.name: Constrained tracking optimal control problem
nodes.statement: Such a control objective can be formalized by the following optimization problem: \begin{eqnarray} & \begin{aligned} \min\limits_{u(0),\hdots,u(T-1)}\sum_{t=0}^{T} &\left( y(t)-y_{\text{des}}(t) \right)^TQ \left( y(t)-y_{\text{des}}(t) \right)+u(t)^T S u(t) + \Delta u(t)^T R \Delta u(t) \end{aligned}\\ &\begin{aligned} & \text{subject to},\,\forall t\in[0,T] \\ &\ba{lllll} Cu(t)&\leq &g\\ L \Delta u(t)&\leq&f\\ E y(t)&\leq& p \ea \end{aligned} \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Minimize a quadratic tracking / input / input-rate cost over horizon $T$ subject to linear input, input-rate and output constraints.

nodes.name: Remark on embedding unmodeled dynamics in the output disturbance
nodes.statement: Note that the influence of the unmodeled dynamics to the plant outputs can be embedded into the output disturbance vector $d(t)$. The facts that the magnitudes of the control inputs are bounded and that the controlled system is stable can be exploited to calculate the bounds on the contribution of the unmodeled dynamics to the plant outputs.

nodes.name: Orthonormal basis function expansion of a stable transfer function
nodes.statement: Any stable transfer function can be represented by the following infinite sum: \beq G(q)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}h(k)\mathcal{L}_k(a,q), \eeq where $q$ is the time shift operator ($qu(t)\doteq u(t+1)$) and $\mathcal{L}_k$ are mutually orthogonal transfer functions characterized by: \beq \frac{1}{2\pi j}\oint \mathcal{L}_p(a,q)\mathcal{L}_k(a,q^{-1})\frac{dq}{q}=\delta_{pk}, \eeq where $\delta_{pk}$ is the Kronecker delta function and the integral is around the unit circle. The parameter $a\in \mathbb{C},\, |a|\leq1$ defines the basis functions. The sequence of coefficients $h(k)$ is convergent as $\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}h(k)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: A stable transfer function expands in a sequence of mutually orthogonal basis transfer functions parametrized by $a$.
nodes.section: Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics
nodes.origin_citation: Wahlberg 1991; Van den Hof, Heuberger & Bokor 1995

nodes.name: Laguerre basis functions
nodes.statement: Basis transfer functions that are usually employed in practice are the Laguerre ones, given as: \beq \mathcal{L}_k(a,q)=\frac{\sqrt{1-a^2}}{q-a}\left[\frac{1-aq}{q-a}\right]^{k-1}, \eeq where $a\in \bR,\, a\in[-1,1]$. If $a$ is selected such that it is close to the dominant pole of the system, only a few coefficients need to be identified in order to have a good model of the system \cite{Laguere}.
nodes.section: Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Kautz basis functions
nodes.statement: For systems that exhibit oscillatory behavior, Kautz functions are more appropriate. These functions have the following form: \beq \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}_{2k-1}(a,q)&=\frac{\sqrt{1\!-\!c^2}(q\!-\!b)}{q^2\!+\!b(c\!-\!1)q\!-\!c}\left[ \frac{-cq^2\!+\!b(c\!-\!1)q\!+\!1}{q^2\!+\!b(c\!-\!1)q\!-\!c}\right]^{k\!-\!1}\\ \mathcal{L}_{2k}(a,q)&=\frac{\sqrt{1\!-\!c^2}(1\!-\!b^2)}{q^2\!+\!b(c\!-\!1)q\!-\!c}\left[ \frac{-cq^2\!+\!b(c\!-\!1)q\!+\!1}{q^2\!+\!b(c\!-\!1)q\!-\!c}\right]_,^{k\!-\!1} \end{aligned} \eeq where $a\in \mathbb{C}, \, |a|\leq1$ and $b=\frac{a+a^*}{1+aa^*}$, $c=-aa^*$ with $^*$ denoting the conjugate of a complex number. Also in this case, the parameter $a$ should be chosen to be close the the dominant oscillatory pole of the system in order to have a system representation that uses only few parameters \cite{Kautz}.
nodes.statement_short: Second-order orthonormal basis functions parametrized by a complex pole $a$, suited to oscillatory systems.
nodes.section: Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Impulse response basis functions
nodes.statement: The impulse response model can be regarded as a special case of a basis function parametrization. The basis functions that give rise to an impulse response model are: \beq \mathcal{L}_k(a,q)=aq^{-k} \eeq
nodes.section: Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics
nodes.definiendum: basis functions that give rise to an impulse response model

nodes.name: Combined impulse response and Laguerre/Kautz parametrization
nodes.statement: In addition, it is possible to use a parametrization that combines the impulse response and Laguerre or Kautz basis functions. In this case the basis functions are defined as: \beq \mathcal{L}_k(a,q)=\begin{cases} q^{-k} & \text{if}\, k\leq n\\ \mathcal{B}_{k-n}(a,q)q^{-n} & \text{if}\, k>n \end{cases}, \eeq where $\mathcal{B}_k(a,q)$ are the Laguerre or Kautz basis functions as defined in \eqref{Eq:Laguere} and \eqref{Eq:Kautz} and $n$ is another design parameter that determines the number of the impulse response coefficients to be used in the modeling. Such a parametrization requires a small number of modeling parameters in the case when the system has a transport delay and if $n$ is selected close to the transport delay time \cite{ydstie}.
nodes.statement_short: First $n$ basis functions are pure delays, the rest are delayed Laguerre/Kautz functions - efficient for transport-delay systems.
nodes.section: Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics
nodes.definiendum: parametrization that combines the impulse response and Laguerre or Kautz basis functions

nodes.name: Assumed structure of the single input-output transfer function $G_{ji}(q)$
nodes.statement: We assume that the transfer function from the input $i$ to the output $j$ has the following structure: \beq G_{ji}(q)=gq^{-\tau}\frac{\prod\limits_{l=1}^{n_z}(q-z_l)}{\prod\limits_{l=1}^{n_p}(q-p_l)}, \eeq where $g\in \bR$ is the gain, $\tau \in \mathbb{N}$, $\tau \geq 0$ is the transport delay, $Z=[z_1,\hdots,z_{n_z}]^T\in \bR^{n_z}$ are the zeros and $P=[p_1,\hdots, p_{n_p}]^T\in \bR^{n_p}$ are the poles of the transfer function.
nodes.section: Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Remark on real poles and zeros
nodes.statement: Note that real poles and zeros are selected here in order to simplify the notation. All the derivations can be extended to the case of general complex poles and zeros.
nodes.section: Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Prior bounds on gain, transport delay, zeros and poles
nodes.statement: We assume that the gain, transport delay, poles and zeros are not exactly known, but they belong to the following set: \beq \ba{ccccc} \underline{g}&\leq & g &\leq &\overline{g}\\ \underline{\tau} & \leq & \tau & \leq & \overline{\tau}\\ \underline{Z}&\leq & Z&\leq &\overline{Z}\\ \underline{P} &\leq & P &\leq &\overline{P} \ea, \eeq where the inequalities in \eqref{Eq:set_of_parameters} should be interpreted as element-wise inequalities and the bounds $\underline{g},\, \overline{g}, \, \underline{\tau}, \, \overline{\tau} \in \bR$, $\underline{Z},\, \overline{Z}\in \bR^{n_z}$ and $\underline{P},\, \overline{P}\in \bR^{n_p}$ are assumed to be known. In addition, it is assumed that $\overline{\tau}\geq 0$ and that the bounds on the poles are selected such that all the poles of the system lay inside the unit circle.
nodes.statement_short: Gain, delay, zeros and poles lie in a known box, with all poles inside the unit circle.
nodes.section: Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Projection of the impulse response onto the basis functions
nodes.statement: Then for any fixed $g$, $\tau$, $Z$ and $P$, the impulse response coefficients $\Psi (g,\tau, Z,P,l)$ can be represented as: \beq \Psi(g,\!\tau,\!Z,\!P,\!l)=\sum\limits_{k=1}^{\infty}h(g,\!\tau,\!Z,\!P,\!k)\Psi_k(a,\,l), \!\forall l=1,\,\hdots,\, \infty, \eeq where, because of the orthogonality of the basis functions, the coefficients $h(g,\tau,Z,P,k)$ are given as normalized projections of $\Psi(g,\tau,Z,P,l)$ on the impulse responses of the basis functions: \beq h(g,\tau,Z,P,k)=\frac{\sum\limits_{l=1}^{\infty}\Psi(g,\tau,Z,P,l)\Psi_k(a,l)}{\sum\limits_{l=1}^{\infty}\Psi_k(a,l)^2}. \eeq
nodes.statement_short: Orthogonality gives the basis coefficients as normalized inner products of the impulse response with the basis impulse responses.
nodes.section: Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Computation of the upper and lower coefficient bounds
nodes.statement: Therefore, the upper and the lower bounds \eqref{Eq:coeficient_bounds} can be calculated as: \beq \begin{aligned} \overline{h}_{ji}(k)&=\sup\limits_{g,\tau,Z,P} h(g,\tau,Z,P,k)\\ \underline{h}_{ji}(k)&=\inf \limits_{g,\tau,Z,P}h(g,\tau,Z,P,k)\\ &\text{subject to \eqref{Eq:set_of_parameters}}, \end{aligned} \eeq
nodes.statement_short: Bound each basis coefficient by maximizing/minimizing its projection over the uncertainty box of $(g,\tau,Z,P)$.
nodes.section: Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Contribution of the unmodeled dynamics $\eta_{ji}(t)$
nodes.statement: The contribution of the unmodeled dynamics on the transfer function from input $i$ to the output $j$ is then given by: \beq \eta_{ji}(t)=\sum\limits_{k=m+1}^{\infty}h_{ji}(k)\zeta \left(\mathcal{L}_k(a,q)u_i(t)\right). \eeq
nodes.section: Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Computation of the bound $\overline{\eta}_{ji}$ on the unmodeled dynamics
nodes.statement: The contribution of the unmodeled dynamics is guaranteed to be bounded: $|\eta(t)|\leq \overline{\eta_{ji}}, \, \forall t$, where the bound $\overline{\eta_{ji}}$ is given by: \beq \begin{aligned} &\overline{\eta}_{ji}=\overline{u_i} \sup\limits_{g,\tau, Z,P}\sum\limits_{l=1}^{\infty}\left|\Psi(g,\!\tau,\! Z,\! P,\! l)-\sum\limits_{k=1}^mh(g,\!\tau,\! Z,\! P,\! k)\Psi_k(a,\! l)\right|\\ &\text{subject to \eqref{Eq:set_of_parameters}} \end{aligned} \eeq where $\overline{u}_i$ can be calculated as: \beq \overline{u}_i=\max\limits_{Cu\leq g}|u_i| \eeq
nodes.statement_short: Bound the truncation error by the worst-case $\ell^1$ residual of the impulse response times the maximal admissible input.
nodes.section: Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Adaptive MPC algorithm
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item[1)]At time step $t$, obtain $\tilde{y}(t)$ and update the model set based on the past applied control inputs and measured plant outputs; \item[2)] Select a nominal model of the plant inside the model set; \item[3)]Calculate a sequence of possible future control inputs by solving a finite horizon optimal control problem (FHOCP) that minimizes the weighted $l_2$ norm of the tracking error for the nominal model and enforces input and output constraints for all the models inside the model set; \item[4)]Apply the first element of the calculated input sequence, set $t=t+1$, go to 1). \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Receding-horizon loop: update the set-membership model set, pick a nominal model, solve the robust FHOCP, apply the first input.
input: the past applied control inputs and measured plant outputs
output: a sequence of possible future control inputs
the first element of the calculated input sequence

nodes.name: Update the model set
nodes.statement: At time step $t$, obtain $\tilde{y}(t)$ and update the model set based on the past applied control inputs and measured plant outputs;
nodes.statement_short: Refine the set-membership model set with the newest measurement.

nodes.name: Select a nominal model
nodes.statement: Select a nominal model of the plant inside the model set;
nodes.statement_short: Pick the central nominal plant model from the current model set.

nodes.name: Solve the FHOCP
nodes.statement: Calculate a sequence of possible future control inputs by solving a finite horizon optimal control problem (FHOCP) that minimizes the weighted $l_2$ norm of the tracking error for the nominal model and enforces input and output constraints for all the models inside the model set;
nodes.statement_short: Solve the robust finite-horizon optimal control problem for the input sequence.

nodes.name: Apply the first input and recede the horizon
nodes.statement: Apply the first element of the calculated input sequence, set $t=t+1$, go to 1).
nodes.statement_short: Apply only the first move, advance time, and loop.

nodes.name: Remark on using the nominal model in the cost function
nodes.statement: Note that an alternative to formulating the cost function based on the tracking error of the nominal model would be to minimize the weighted $l_2$ norm of the worst case tracking error for all the models inside the model set. The drawback of this approach is that if the prior assumptions were not informative enough, the model set would be initially large due to high uncertainty, and then the applied control inputs would be very small in magnitude. Such control inputs would in turn not be very informative, therefore the size of the model set would reduce slowly, hence resulting in a very conservative controller.
nodes.statement_short: Min-max tracking over the model set would yield uninformative, overly conservative inputs, hence the nominal-model cost.

nodes.name: Recursive computation of the regressor vector
nodes.statement: The regressor vector $\varphi(l)$ can be calculated recursively as: \begin{equation} \varphi(l)=W\varphi(l-1)+Zu(l-1), \end{equation} where $W\in \bR^{n_um \times n_um}$ and $Z \in \bR^{n_um\times n_u}$ are suitable matrices that depend on the selected basis function parametrization.

nodes.name: Model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$
nodes.statement: At a given time step $t$, we define the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$ as the set containing all the matrices $H$ that are consistent with the Assumptions \ref{A:disturbance} and \ref{A:system_class} and the collected input-output data \eqref{Eq:measured_data}: \beq \begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}(t)\!\doteq\! \left\{\ba{ll} H\!\in\! \mathcal{F}(0)\!:\!&-\epsilon_d\!-\!\epsilon_v\leq \tilde{y}(l)\!-\!H\varphi(l)\leq \epsilon_d\!+\!\epsilon_v,\,\forall l \in [0,t] \ea\right\}\!\!. \end{aligned} \eeq
nodes.statement_short: The feasible parameter set of all models consistent with the priors and all data up to time $t$.
nodes.genus: the set containing all the matrices $H$
differentia: that are consistent with the Assumptions \ref{A:disturbance} and \ref{A:system_class} and the collected input-output data

nodes.name: Polytopic representation of the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$
nodes.statement: Since the initial model set $\mathcal{F}(0)$ is defined by polytopic constraints on each row $H_j^T$ of the matrix $H$, and the constraints in \eqref{Eq:FSSm_t} are linear, the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$ is still defined by polytopic constraints on $H_j^T,\, j=1,\hdots n_y$. Each of these polytopes can be uniquely described by a set of non-redundant inequalities. Therefore, at a generic time step $t$, the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$ can be represented as: \beq \mathcal{F}(t)\!=\! \left\{H\!\in\!\bR^{n_y \times n_um}\!:\!A_j(t)H_{j}\leq b_j(t),\, j=1,\hdots, n_y \right\}, \eeq where $A_j(t) \in \bR^{r_j(t) \times n_um}$, $b_j(t) \in \bR^{r_j(t)}$ and $r_j(t)$ is the number of non-redundant inequalities pertaining to the $j^\text{th}$ row of the matrix $H$.
nodes.statement_short: The model set stays a row-wise polytope, representable by non-redundant inequalities $A_j(t)H_j\leq b_j(t)$.
assumptions: the initial model set $\mathcal{F}(0)$ is defined by polytopic constraints on each row $H_j^T$ of the matrix $H$
conclusions: the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$ is still defined by polytopic constraints on $H_j^T,\, j=1,\hdots n_y$

nodes.name: Row-wise polytopes $\mathcal{F}_j(t)$
nodes.statement: The matrices $A_j(t)$ and the vectors $b_j(t)$ have to be updated at each time step in order to account for the new measurements. To this end, let us consider the following polytopes: \beq \mathcal{F}_j(t)=\{H_j\in \bR^{n_um}: A_j(t)H_j\leq b_j(t)\},\, j=1\hdots n_y. \eeq

nodes.name: Recursive polytopic model set update
nodes.statement: We note that for each $j$, the polytope $\mathcal{F}_{j}(t)$ can be calculated recursively in time as the intersection of the polytope $\mathcal{F}_{j}(t-1)$ and the two half spaces defined by the newly measured plant output, $\tilde{y}_j(t)$: \beq \begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}_{j}(t)= &\mathcal{F}_{j}(t-1) \\ &\cap \{H_{j}\!\!\in\!\bR^{n_um}\!:\!\varphi(t)^TH_{j}\leq \tilde{y}_j(t)\!+\!\epsilon_{d_j}\!+\!\epsilon_{v_j}\}\\ &\cap \{H_{j}\!\!\in\!\bR^{n_um}\!:\! -\varphi(t)^TH_{j}\leq -\tilde{y}_j(t)\!+\!\epsilon_{d_j}\!+\!\epsilon_{v_j}\}. \end{aligned} \eeq
nodes.statement_short: Each new measurement intersects the previous polytope with two data half-spaces.

nodes.name: Nominal model $H_c(t)$ (Chebyshev centers of the polytopes)
nodes.statement: In addition to the model set, the proposed SM identification algorithm also provides a nominal model of the plant (step 2) of Algorithm \ref{Alg:RHCOP2}). The latter is given by a matrix $H_{c}(t)\in \bR^{n_y\times n_um}$, $H_c=[H_{c,1},\hdots H_{c,n_y}]^T$, where $H_{c,j}(t)\in \bR^{n_um},\, j=1,\hdots, n_y$ are computed as the centers of the maximum volume $l_2$-norm balls inscribed in the polytopes $\mathcal{F}_{j}(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: The nominal model rows are the centers of the largest $\ell_2$ balls inscribed in the row polytopes.
differentia: $H_{c,j}(t)\in \bR^{n_um},\, j=1,\hdots, n_y$ are computed as the centers of the maximum volume $l_2$-norm balls inscribed in the polytopes $\mathcal{F}_{j}(t)$

nodes.name: Regularized LP for the nominal model
nodes.statement: This can be done by solving an LP, however the solution is not unique in general. Therefore, we introduce a regularization term, that penalizes the deviation of the new nominal model from the previous one, giving rise to the following LP: \beq \ba{c} \max \limits_{\xi_j(t),H_{c,j}(t)} \sum \limits_{j=1}^{n_y}\xi_j(t)-\alpha\|H_{c,j}(t-1)-H_{c,j}(t)\|_1\\ \text{subject to}\\ a_{ji}(t)H_{c,j}(t)\!+\!\xi_j(t)\|a_{ji}(t)\|_2\!\leq\! b_{ji}(t), \, j=1,\hdots, n_y,\, i=1,\hdots, n_u, \ea \eeq where $\xi_j(t) \in \bR$ is the radius of the maximum volume ball inscribed in $\mathcal{F}_{j}(t)$, $\alpha>0$ is a design variable, and $a_{ji}(t)$ and $b_{ji}(t)$ stand for the $i^{\text{th}}$ row of the matrix $A_j(t)$ and the vector $b_j(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Maximize the inscribed-ball radii minus an $\ell_1$ penalty on nominal-model movement, subject to polytope face constraints.

nodes.name: Future control moves and input increments $\Delta u(k|t)$
nodes.statement: Let $u(k|t),\, k\in[t,t+N-1]$, $N\geq m$, be the possible future control moves, where the notation $k|t$ indicates the prediction at step $k\geq t$ given the information at the current step $t$. Similarly, we define the vectors of future input increments $\Delta u(k|t), \, k\in [t,t+N-1]$ as: \beq \!\Delta u(k|t)\!=\!\begin{cases} u(t|t)\!-\!u(t-1)\!\! & \text{if}\, k=t\\ u(k|t)\!-\!u(k\!-\!1|t)\!\! & \text{if}\, t\!+\!1\leq k\leq t\!+\!N\!-\!1 \end{cases} \eeq
nodes.statement_short: Predicted inputs over the horizon and their first differences.

nodes.name: Predicted future regressor vectors
nodes.statement: Moreover, we define the future regressor vectors $\varphi(k|t)\in\bR^{n_um},\,k\in[t+1,t+N]$ as: \begin{equation} \varphi(k|t)\!=\!\!\begin{cases} W\varphi(t)\!\!+\!\!Zu(t|t)\!\!\! & \text{if} \,\, k=t+1\\ W \varphi(k\!-\!1|t)\!\!+\!\!Zu(k\!-\!1|t) \!\!\!& \text{if} \,\, t\!+\!2\!\leq\! k\!\leq\! t\!+\!N. \end{cases} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Current prediction error $\hat{d}(t)$
nodes.statement: In addition, we define the current prediction error $\hat{d}(t)\in \bR^{n_y}$ as the difference between the measured plant output and the one predicted by the nominal model at the time step $t$: \beq \hat{d}(t)\doteq \tilde{y}(t)-H_c(t)\varphi(t). \eeq
nodes.genus: the difference between the measured plant output and the one predicted by the nominal model at the time step $t$

nodes.name: Finite horizon cost function $J(U,\tilde{y}(t),\varphi(t))$
nodes.statement: Then, we consider the following cost function: \beq \begin{aligned} J(U,\tilde{y}(t),\varphi(t))\doteq \sum\limits_{k=t}^{t\!+\!N\!-\!1}\!&\!\left(\hat{y}(k\!+\!1|t)\!-\!y_{\text{des}}(k\!+\!1|t)\right)^TQ(\hat{y}(k\!+\!1|t)-\!y_{\text{des}}(k\!+\!1|t))\!+\! u(k|t)^TSu(k|t)\\&+\Delta u(k|t)^TR\Delta u(k|t), \end{aligned}\!\! \eeq where: \beq \hat{y}(k+1|t)=H_c(t)\varphi(k+1|t)+\hat{d}(t). \eeq
nodes.statement_short: Quadratic horizon cost on nominal tracking error, input and input rate, with the nominal output offset by $\hat{d}(t)$.
differentia: sum over $k\in[t,t+N-1]$ of weighted nominal tracking error, input and input-increment terms

nodes.name: Input and input-rate constraints over the prediction horizon
nodes.statement: Satisfaction of input constraints can be enforced by the following set of inequalities: \beq \ba{ll} \begin{aligned} C u(k|t) & \leq & d\\ L \Delta u(k|t) & \leq & f \end{aligned} & \forall k\in[t,t+N-1]. \ea \eeq

nodes.name: Robust output constraints over the model set
nodes.statement: And the robust satisfaction of the output constraints can be achieved by enforcing the latter for all the plants inside the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$ and all disturbance realizations: \beq E(H\varphi(k|t)\!+\!d)\leq p, \, \ba{l}\forall H\! \in\! \mathcal{F}(t),\, \forall d: -\epsilon_d\leq d\leq \epsilon_d,\\ \forall k\in[t\!+\!1,t\!+\!N] \ea \eeq The constraints \eqref{Eq:output1} are satisfied for anny disturbance realization if the following set of inequalities is satisfied: \beq EH\varphi(k|t)\!+\!\overline{d}\leq p, \, \forall H\! \in\! \mathcal{F}(t),\, \forall k\in[t\!+\!1,t\!+\!N], \eeq where $\overline{d}=[\overline{d}_1,\hdots, \overline{d}_{n_o}]^T$, and $d_l \in \bR,\, l=1,\hdots, n_o$ are given as: \beq \overline{d}_l=\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n_y}|e_{lj}|\epsilon_{d_j}, \eeq where $e_{lj}$ stand for the element of the $l^\text{th}$ row and $j^\text{th}$ column of the matrix $E$.
nodes.statement_short: Output constraints tightened by the worst-case disturbance $\overline{d}$ must hold for every model in $\mathcal{F}(t)$.

nodes.name: Lemma 1 (LP-duality reformulation of the robust output constraints)
nodes.statement: The constraints (\ref{Eq:output}) are satisfied if and only if the following set of inequalities is feasible: \small \beq \left.\ba{l}\!\! A(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)=\left[\ba{c} e_{l1}\varphi(k|t)\\ \vdots\\ e_{ln_y}\varphi(k|t) \ea\right]\\ b(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)\leq p_l\!-\!\overline{d}_l\\ \lambda_l(k|t)\geq \bold 0 \ea \right\}\ba{cc}\forall l=1,\hdots,n_o\\ \forall k\!\in\![t\!+\!1,t\!+\!N]\ea \eeq \normalsize with \small \beq \begin{aligned} A(t)&=\left[\ba{cccc} A_1(t)& \bold 0& \ldots&\bold 0\\ \bold 0& A_2(t)& \ldots& \bold 0\\ \vdots& \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \bold 0&\bold 0& \ldots&A_{n_y}(t)\ea \right]\\ b(t)&=\left[\ba{c} b_1(t)\\ \vdots\\ b_{n_y}(t) \ea \right], \end{aligned} \eeq \normalsize where $\bold 0$ represents zero matrices of appropriate dimensions and $j^\text{th}$ column of the matrix $E$ and $p_l$ is the $l^\text{th}$ element of the vector $p$. In \eqref{Eq:relaxed_constraints1}, $\lambda_l(k|t) \in \bR^{r(t)}$ are additional decision variables, where $r(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{n_y} r_j(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: The semi-infinite robust output constraints are equivalent to a finite set of linear constraints on LP dual multipliers $\lambda_l(k|t)$.
assumptions: $\lambda_l(k|t) \in \bR^{r(t)}$ are additional decision variables, where $r(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{n_y} r_j(t)$
conclusions: the following set of inequalities is feasible: $A(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)=\left[\ba{c} e_{l1}\varphi(k|t)\\ \vdots\\ e_{ln_y}\varphi(k|t) \ea\right]$, $b(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)\leq p_l\!-\!\overline{d}_l$, $\lambda_l(k|t)\geq \bold 0$, $\forall l=1,\hdots,n_o$, $\forall k\!\in\![t\!+\!1,t\!+\!N]$

nodes.name: Strong duality theorem for LPs
nodes.statement: According to the strong duality theorem for LPs \cite{LP_book}, it holds that: $\gamma_l(k)=\tilde{\gamma}_l(k)$.
nodes.statement_short: The primal and dual optima of the LP over the model-set polytope coincide.
assumptions: the inequalities $A_j(t) H_j\leq b_j(t),\, j=1,\hdots, n_y$ form nonempty, closed and bounded convex sets (i.e. polytopes)

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: We first note that, from the definition of the set $\mathcal{F}(t)$, it follows that constraints \eqref{Eq:output} are satisfied if and only if the following set of inequalities is satisfied: \beq \ba{ll} \gamma_l(k)\leq p_l\!-\!\overline{d}_l, & \ba{c} \forall l=1,\hdots,n_o\\\forall k\in [t+1,t+N]\ea\ea \eeq where \beq \gamma_l(k)=\max \limits_{A_j(t)H_j\leq b_j(t)}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n_y}e_{lj}\varphi(k|t)^TH_j. \eeq For fixed values of the vectors $\varphi(k|t), \, k\in [t+1,t+N]$, by using the fact that the inequalities $A_j(t) H_j\leq b_j(t),\, j=1,\hdots, n_y$ form nonempty, closed and bounded convex sets (i.e. polytopes), we can write the dual of the LP \eqref{Eq:Linear_proggrams_1} as: \bea &\tilde{\gamma}_l(k)=\min \limits_{\lambda_l(k|t)}b(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)\\ &\text{subject to} \nonumber\\ &A(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)=\left[ \ba{c} e_{l1}\varphi(k|t)\\ \vdots\\ e_{ln_y}\varphi(k|t)\ea\right]\\ &\lambda_l(k|t)\geq \bold 0 . \eea According to the strong duality theorem for LPs \cite{LP_book}, it holds that: $\gamma_l(k)=\tilde{\gamma}_l(k)$. Therefore, for any $\lambda_l(k|t)$ that satisfies the constraints (\ref{Eq:LP1c1}) and \eqref{Eq:LP1c2}, it holds that $\gamma_l(k) \leq b(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)$. Hence the existence of $\varphi(k|t)$ and $\lambda_l(k|t)$ that satisfy the set of constraints (\ref{Eq:relaxed_constraints1}) guarantees that the constraints (\ref{Eq:LP1}) are also satisfied, which implies the satisfaction of the original constraints \eqref{Eq:output}. On the other hand if the constraints \eqref{Eq:output} are satisfied, then there exists $\gamma_l(k)$ satisfying \eqref{Eq:LP1}. Then by the strong duality theorem for LP, $\tilde{\gamma}_l(k)=\gamma_l(k)$ exists and hence the constraints \eqref{Eq:LP1c1} and \eqref{Eq:LP1c2} have to be feasible, which implies the feasibility of \eqref{Eq:relaxed_constraints1}. \hfill$\blacksquare$
nodes.statement_short: Recast the worst-case output as an LP over the polytope, dualize it, and use LP strong duality for both implications.

nodes.name: Recast robust constraints as worst-case LP values
nodes.statement: We first note that, from the definition of the set $\mathcal{F}(t)$, it follows that constraints \eqref{Eq:output} are satisfied if and only if the following set of inequalities is satisfied: \beq \ba{ll} \gamma_l(k)\leq p_l\!-\!\overline{d}_l, & \ba{c} \forall l=1,\hdots,n_o\\\forall k\in [t+1,t+N]\ea\ea \eeq where \beq \gamma_l(k)=\max \limits_{A_j(t)H_j\leq b_j(t)}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n_y}e_{lj}\varphi(k|t)^TH_j. \eeq
nodes.statement_short: Set up: replace the $\forall H$ constraint by the maximal value $\gamma_l(k)$ of an LP over the model set.

nodes.name: Form the LP dual
nodes.statement: For fixed values of the vectors $\varphi(k|t), \, k\in [t+1,t+N]$, by using the fact that the inequalities $A_j(t) H_j\leq b_j(t),\, j=1,\hdots, n_y$ form nonempty, closed and bounded convex sets (i.e. polytopes), we can write the dual of the LP \eqref{Eq:Linear_proggrams_1} as: \bea &\tilde{\gamma}_l(k)=\min \limits_{\lambda_l(k|t)}b(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)\\ &\text{subject to} \nonumber\\ &A(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)=\left[ \ba{c} e_{l1}\varphi(k|t)\\ \vdots\\ e_{ln_y}\varphi(k|t)\ea\right]\\ &\lambda_l(k|t)\geq \bold 0 . \eea
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the dual multipliers $\lambda_l(k|t)$ and write the dual LP.

nodes.name: Sufficiency via strong duality
nodes.statement: According to the strong duality theorem for LPs \cite{LP_book}, it holds that: $\gamma_l(k)=\tilde{\gamma}_l(k)$. Therefore, for any $\lambda_l(k|t)$ that satisfies the constraints (\ref{Eq:LP1c1}) and \eqref{Eq:LP1c2}, it holds that $\gamma_l(k) \leq b(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)$. Hence the existence of $\varphi(k|t)$ and $\lambda_l(k|t)$ that satisfy the set of constraints (\ref{Eq:relaxed_constraints1}) guarantees that the constraints (\ref{Eq:LP1}) are also satisfied, which implies the satisfaction of the original constraints \eqref{Eq:output}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply LP strong duality to show feasibility of the dual constraints implies the original robust constraints.

nodes.name: Necessity direction
nodes.statement: On the other hand if the constraints \eqref{Eq:output} are satisfied, then there exists $\gamma_l(k)$ satisfying \eqref{Eq:LP1}. Then by the strong duality theorem for LP, $\tilde{\gamma}_l(k)=\gamma_l(k)$ exists and hence the constraints \eqref{Eq:LP1c1} and \eqref{Eq:LP1c2} have to be feasible, which implies the feasibility of \eqref{Eq:relaxed_constraints1}.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the converse: robust satisfaction forces the dual constraint set to be feasible.

nodes.name: Terminal steady-state constraint
nodes.statement: In order to be able to recursively satisfy the input and output constraints, we introduce an additional constraint on the terminal stage: \beq \varphi(t+N|t)=W\varphi(t+N|t)+Zu(t+N-1|t). \eeq This means that we require the terminal regressor to correspond to a steady state.

nodes.name: Finite horizon optimal control problem (FHOCP)
nodes.statement: For fixed values of $N$, $Q$, $S$ and $R$, we can now define the finite horizon optimal control problem (FHOCP) to be solved at time step $t$ (see step 3) of Algorithm \ref{Alg:RHCOP2}): \beq \begin{aligned} \min \limits_{U} &J(U,\tilde{y}(t),\varphi (t))\\ &\text{subject to}\, \eqref{Eq:input_rate},\, \eqref{Eq:relaxed_constraints1}, \, \eqref{Eq:end_constraint}, \end{aligned} \eeq which is a quadratic program (QP), that can be efficiently solved.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize the nominal horizon cost $J$ subject to input, dualized robust output and terminal constraints - a QP.

nodes.name: Recursive feasibility and constraint satisfaction of the adaptive control algorithm
nodes.statement: The proposed adaptive control algorithm is such that if the problem \eqref{Eq:FHOCP} that is solved under Algorithm \ref{Alg:RHCOP2} has a feasible solution at time step $0$, then it is guaranteed to have a feasible solution $\forall t\geq 0$. This means that the proposed adaptive control algorithm guarantees the satisfaction of both input and output constraints $\forall t$.
nodes.statement_short: Initial feasibility implies feasibility for all times, hence constraints hold at all times.
assumptions: the problem \eqref{Eq:FHOCP} that is solved under Algorithm \ref{Alg:RHCOP2} has a feasible solution at time step $0$
conclusions: it is guaranteed to have a feasible solution $\forall t\geq 0$
the proposed adaptive control algorithm guarantees the satisfaction of both input and output constraints $\forall t$

nodes.name: Two-stage control input calculation with exploring property
nodes.statement: A possible method to add an exploring property to the control algorithm is to split the calculation of the control input in two stages. In the first stage, the FHOCP \eqref{Eq:FHOCP} is solved as usual. The computed optimal control sequence and the knowledge of the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$ are then used to calculate the upper bounds, along the chosen prediction horizon, on the absolute difference between all the possible future outputs of the plant and the nominal optimal output trajectory. In the second stage, by allowing these bounds to be inflated by a factor selected by the control designer, the sequence of control inputs can then be recalculated in order to improve the reduction in size of the model set. To this end, the control input is selected such that it approximately minimizes the volume of the polytopes that will form the model set at the next time step, while at the same time ensuring that the difference between the future trajectory of the plant outputs and the optimal one calculated in the first stage remains inside the selected bounds, and that the input and output constraints are satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the tracking FHOCP, then re-optimize the input for excitation within inflated output-trajectory tubes.
nodes.section: Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
input: the knowledge of the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$
a factor selected by the control designer
output: the sequence of control inputs can then be recalculated in order to improve the reduction in size of the model set

nodes.name: First stage: solve the FHOCP and compute output bounds
nodes.statement: In the first stage, the FHOCP \eqref{Eq:FHOCP} is solved as usual. The computed optimal control sequence and the knowledge of the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$ are then used to calculate the upper bounds, along the chosen prediction horizon, on the absolute difference between all the possible future outputs of the plant and the nominal optimal output trajectory.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the tracking problem and size the uncertainty tube around its predicted output trajectory.
nodes.section: Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm

nodes.name: Second stage: re-optimize the input for exploration
nodes.statement: In the second stage, by allowing these bounds to be inflated by a factor selected by the control designer, the sequence of control inputs can then be recalculated in order to improve the reduction in size of the model set. To this end, the control input is selected such that it approximately minimizes the volume of the polytopes that will form the model set at the next time step, while at the same time ensuring that the difference between the future trajectory of the plant outputs and the optimal one calculated in the first stage remains inside the selected bounds, and that the input and output constraints are satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: Recompute the input to shrink the next model set while staying inside the inflated tube and the constraints.
nodes.section: Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm

nodes.name: Maximal predicted output deviation $\overline{\epsilon}_j(k|t)$
nodes.statement: We denote the predicted regressor vectors and plant outputs obtained by solving \eqref{Eq:FHOCP} by $\varphi'(k|t)$ and $\hat{y}'(k|t),\, k\in[t+1,t+N]$. Then for the second stage, we compute the following quantities: \beq \begin{aligned} \overline{\epsilon}_j(k|t)=&\max \left\{ \overline{y}_j(k|t)-\hat{y}'_j(k|t),\, \hat{y}'_j(k|t)-\underline{y}_j(k|t) \right \}, k\in [t+1,t+N],\,\, j=1,\hdots, n_y, \end{aligned} \eeq where $\overline{\epsilon}(k|t)=[\overline{\epsilon}_1(k|t),\hdots, \overline{\epsilon}_{n_y}(k|t)]^T$, $\overline{\epsilon}_j(k|t)\geq 0$ denotes the maximal possible difference between the possible future output of the plant and the predicted output at time step $k$, and \beq \ba{ccc} \overline{y}_j(k|t)&=&\max\limits_{A_j(t)H_j\leq b_j(t)} H_j^T\varphi'(k|t)\\ \underline{y}_j(k|t)&=& \min\limits_{A_j(t)H_j\leq b_j(t)} H_j^T\varphi'(k|t). \ea \eeq
nodes.statement_short: Half-width of the interval of outputs consistent with the model set, measured around the first-stage predicted trajectory.
nodes.section: Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
nodes.genus: the maximal possible difference between the possible future output of the plant and the predicted output at time step $k$
differentia: $\overline{y}_j(k|t)$ and $\underline{y}_j(k|t)$ are the max and min of $H_j^T\varphi'(k|t)$ over $A_j(t)H_j\leq b_j(t)$

nodes.name: Regressor matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)$
nodes.statement: In addition, we define the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)\in \bR^{n_um\times n_um}$ that depends on the $n_um$ past regressor vectors and the first future regressor vector as: \beq \Phi(t+1|t)=\left[\ba{cccc} \varphi(t-n_um+1) &\hdots & \varphi(t) & \varphi(t+1|t) \ea \right]. \eeq
nodes.section: Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
differentia: depends on the $n_um$ past regressor vectors and the first future regressor vector

nodes.name: Lemma 2 (volume bound on the updated polytopes)
nodes.statement: Each of the polytopes $\mathcal{F}_j(t+1),\, j=1,\hdots,n_y$ obtained by using the polytopic update of the form \eqref{Eq:Normal_update} for a sequence of control input vectors that define the regressor vectors forming the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)$ is guaranteed to have the volume smaller than $\frac{\left(2(\epsilon_{d_j}+\epsilon_{v_j})\right)^{n_um}}{\left| \det\left( \Phi(t+1|t)\right)\right|}$.\hfill$\blacksquare$
nodes.statement_short: The next model-set polytope volume is bounded by a noise term divided by $|\det \Phi(t+1|t)|$.
assumptions: the polytopes $\mathcal{F}_j(t+1),\, j=1,\hdots,n_y$ obtained by using the polytopic update of the form \eqref{Eq:Normal_update}
a sequence of control input vectors that define the regressor vectors forming the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)$
conclusions: is guaranteed to have the volume smaller than $\frac{\left(2(\epsilon_{d_j}+\epsilon_{v_j})\right)^{n_um}}{\left| \det\left( \Phi(t+1|t)\right)\right|}$
nodes.section: Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm

nodes.name: Second-stage exploring optimization problem
nodes.statement: Therefore, the optimization problem to be solved at the second stage of the control input calculation is given as: \beq \begin{aligned} &\max \limits_U \left|\det \Phi(t+1|t) \right|\\ &\text {subject to}\\ &\eqref{Eq:input_rate}, \, \eqref{Eq:end_constraint},\\ &\left.\ba{lll} H\varphi(k|t)&\!\leq\!& \hat{y}'(k|t)\!+\!r\overline{\epsilon}(k|t)\\ H\varphi(k|t)&\!\geq\! &\hat{y}'(k|t)\!-\!r\overline{\epsilon}(k|t)\\ EH\varphi(k|t)\!+\!\overline{d}&\! \leq\!&\! p \ea \right\}\ba{ll}\forall H\in \mathcal{F}(t)\\ \forall k\in[t\!+\!1, t\!+\!N] \ea \end{aligned} \eeq where $r\in \bR$, $r\geq 1$ is a design parameter, selected by the control designer, that determines the allowed augmentation of the intervals containing the predicted outputs between the first and second stages.
nodes.statement_short: Maximize $|\det \Phi(t+1|t)|$ subject to input, terminal, tube and robust output constraints.
nodes.section: Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm

nodes.name: Augmented constraint matrices $E''$, $\overline{d''}$ and $p''(k|t)$
nodes.statement: In fact, if we define the matrix $E''$ and the vectors $\overline{d''}$ and $p''(k|t),\, k\in [t+1,t+N]$ as: \beq E''=\left[ \ba{c} I\\ -I\\ E \ea \right],\, \overline{d''}=\left[\ba{c} \bold{0}\\ \bold{0}\\ \overline{d} \ea \right],\, p''(k|t)=\left[ \ba{c} \hat{y}'(k|t)\!+\!r\overline{\epsilon}(k|t)\\-\hat{y}'(k|t)\!+\!r\overline{\epsilon}(k|t)\\p\ea \right], \eeq where $I$ and $\bold{0}$ respectively denote the identity and zero matrices of apropriate size, then the infinite dimensional constraints in \eqref{Eq:FHOCP2_cost} can be rewritten as \beq E''H\varphi(k|t)\!+\!\overline{d''}\leq p''(k|t),\, \forall H\in \mathcal{F}(t),\, k\in[t\!+\!1,t\!+\!N], \eeq and these constraints can be written in the form of linear constraints by using the Lemma \ref{L:constraint_equivalence_1}.
nodes.statement_short: Stack tube and output constraints into a single $E''$-form so Lemma 1 applies verbatim.
nodes.section: Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
nodes.genus: matrix and vectors defining the augmented output constraints

nodes.name: Determinant of $\Phi(t+1|t)$ is affine in the first future input
nodes.statement: In addition, we note that from the definition of the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)$ and the regressor vector $\varphi(t+1|t)$, it follows that the determinant of the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)$ can be expressed as a linear function of the first future control input as: \beq \det\left(\Phi(t+1|t)\right)=k^T u(t|t)+n, \eeq where the derivation of $k \in \bR^{n_u}$ and $n \in \bR$ is given in the Appendix \ref{S:alpha_beta}.
nodes.statement_short: $\det \Phi(t+1|t)$ is affine in $u(t|t)$, with coefficients derived in the appendix.
assumptions: from the definition of the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)$ and the regressor vector $\varphi(t+1|t)$
conclusions: the determinant of the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)$ can be expressed as a linear function of the first future control input as: $\det\left(\Phi(t+1|t)\right)=k^T u(t|t)+n$
nodes.section: Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm

nodes.name: Pair of LPs replacing the second-stage problem
nodes.statement: Therefore, the optimization problem \eqref{Eq:FHOCP2_cost} can be solved by first solving the following two LPs: \bea J_1=\max \limits_{u(k|t)} k^T u(t|t)\\ J_2=\min \limits_{u(k|t)} k^T u(t|t) \eea \beq \ba{l} \text{subject to}\\ \eqref{Eq:input_rate}, \, \eqref{Eq:end_constraint},\\ \left.\ba{l}\!\! A(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)=\left[\ba{c} e_{l1}''\varphi(k|t)\\ \vdots\\ e_{ln_y}''\varphi(k|t) \ea\right]\\ b(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)\leq p_l''(k|t)\!-\!\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n_y}e_{lj}''\epsilon_{d_j}\\ \lambda_l(k|t)\geq \bold 0 \ea\!\!\! \right\}\ba{cc}\forall l=1,\!\hdots,\!n_o\!+\!2n_y\\ \forall k\!\in\![t\!+\!1,t\!+\!N]\ea \ea \eeq where $e_{lj}''$ stand for the element of the $l^\text{th}$ row and $j^\text{th}$ column of the matrix $E''$ and $p_l''(k|t)$ is the $l^\text{th}$ element of the vector $p''(k|t)$. The matrix $A(t)$ and the vector $b(t)$ are defined as in \eqref{Eq:explanation}.
nodes.statement_short: Maximize and minimize the affine determinant surrogate $k^Tu(t|t)$ over the dualized linear constraint set.
nodes.section: Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm

nodes.name: Selection rule between the two LP solutions
nodes.statement: The solution to \eqref{Eq:FHOCP2_cost} can then be obtained by comparing the cost function values of the two LPs: if $|J_1+n|\leq |J_2+n|$, then the solution of the LP with the cost function \eqref{Eq:cost1} is the solution of the original problem and vice-versa. Initially, at time step $t=0$, the regressor vectors that form the matrix $\Phi(1|0)$ can be constructed from the constraints that form the initial model set $\mathcal{F}(0)$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick whichever of the two LP optima gives the larger $|{\cdot}+n|$ to recover the non-convex maximizer.
conclusions: the solution of the LP with the cost function \eqref{Eq:cost1} is the solution of the original problem and vice-versa
nodes.section: Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm

nodes.name: Tractability and recursive feasibility of the exploring extension
nodes.statement: The proposed extension is computationally tractable as it requires the additional solution of two LPs. Moreover, the optimization problem that is solved in the second stage of the control input calculation is guaranteed to be recursively feasible, since the solution obtained in the first stage is always a feasible solution for the second stage. Due to this, the proposed extension allows us to retain the guarantee of constraint satisfaction for all time.
nodes.statement_short: Two extra LPs suffice, and the first-stage solution certifies recursive feasibility of the second stage.
assumptions: the solution obtained in the first stage is always a feasible solution for the second stage
conclusions: the optimization problem that is solved in the second stage of the control input calculation is guaranteed to be recursively feasible
the proposed extension allows us to retain the guarantee of constraint satisfaction for all time
nodes.section: Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm

nodes.name: Remark on the approximation in the exploring cost function
nodes.statement: The cost function \eqref{Eq:FHOCP2_cost} only approximately minimizes the volume of the polytopes that will form the model set in the next time step. In order to have exact minimization, all the collected control inputs and the effects of the limited polytopic update algorithm would need to be taken into account. However, the resulting optimization problem would then be computationally intractable. In addition, the cost function minimizes only the volume of the polytopes in the next time step and not over the whole prediction horizon, as this would also lead to a computationally intractable optimization problem. Despite these approximations, the proposed modification gives good results in practice, as shown by the numerical example.
nodes.statement_short: The determinant surrogate is only an approximate, one-step volume minimizer, traded off against tractability.
nodes.section: Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm

nodes.name: Matrices $W$ and $Z$ for the impulse response parametrization
nodes.statement: For the case when impulse response parametrization is used ($\mathcal{L}_k(a,q)$ is given by \eqref{Eq:impulse_response}), we define the matrix $w\in \bR^{n_u \times n_u}$ with the following structure: \begin{equation*} w=\left[ \ba{ccccc} 0 & 0 & \hdots & 0 & 0\\ a & 0 & \hdots & 0 & 0\\ 0 & a & \hdots & 0 & 0\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots\\ 0 & 0 & \hdots & a & 0 \ea \right] \in \bR^{m\times m}. \end{equation*} Based on this, the matrix $W$ is given by: \begin{equation} W=\left[\ba{cccc} w &\bold{0} & \hdots & \bold{0}\\ \bold{0} & w & \hdots & \bold{0}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ \bold{0} & \bold{0} & \hdots & w \ea\right] \in \bR^{n_um \times n_um}, \end{equation} where $\bold{0}$ denotes the matrix of all zeros with appropriate dimension. Similarly, in order to define the matrix $Z\in \bR^{n_um\times n_u}$, we first define the vector $z=[a,0,\hdots,0]^T\in \bR^m$. Then we can write the matrix $Z$ as: \begin{equation} Z=\left[\ba{cccc} z & \bold{0} & \hdots & \bold{0}\\ \bold{0} & z & \hdots & \bold {0}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \bold{0} & \bold{0} & \hdots & z \ea \right]\in \bR^{n_um\times n_u}, \end{equation} where $\bold{0}$ denotes the vector of all zeros of dimension $m$.
nodes.statement_short: Block-diagonal shift matrices $W$ and input matrices $Z$ realizing the impulse-response regressor recursion.
nodes.genus: block diagonal matrices built from $w$ and $z$
differentia: $w$ is the shift matrix with $a$ on the subdiagonal

nodes.name: Matrices $W$ and $Z$ for the Laguerre parametrization
nodes.statement: For the case when Laguerre basis functions are used for parametrization ($\mathcal{L}_k(a,q)$ is given by \eqref{Eq:Laguere}), we define the matrix $w \in \bR^{m\times m}$ as: \begin{equation*} w=\left[\ba{ccccc} a & 0 & 0 & \hdots & 0\\ 1-a^2 & a & 0 &\hdots & 0\\ (-a)(1-a^2) & 1-a^2 & a & \hdots & 0\\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ (-a)^{m-2}(1-a^2) & (-a)^{m-3}(1-a^2)& \hdots &\hdots& a \ea \right]. \end{equation*} The matrix $W$ is then defined as in \eqref{Eq:W}. The vector $z\in \bR^m$ is defined as: \begin{equation*} z=\sqrt{1-a^2}\left[\ba{c} 1\\-a\\(-a)^2\\ \hdots \\ (-a)^{m-1} \ea \right]\in \bR^m, \end{equation*} and $Z$ is given as in \eqref{Eq:Z}. For the Kautz basis functions, the matrices can be derived in a similar way, but have a more complex structure. In the case when the combination of impulse response and basis function parametrization is used, the matrices can easily be derived along the lines presented here.
nodes.statement_short: Lower-triangular Laguerre state matrix $w$ and geometric input vector $z$ giving $W$ and $Z$.
nodes.definiendum: matrices $W$ and $Z$ for the Laguerre parametrization
nodes.genus: block diagonal matrices built from $w$ and $z$
differentia: $w$ is the lower-triangular Laguerre matrix with $a$ on the diagonal

nodes.name: Determinant of a square matrix
nodes.statement: In order to define $k \in \bR^{n_u}$ and $n \in \bR$, we first shortly recall the definition of the matrix determinant. For a square matrix $A\in \bR^{N\times N}$, the determinant is defined as: \beq \det (A)=\sum \limits_{\sigma \in S_N}\sgn(\sigma) \prod \limits_{i=1}^N A_{i,\sigma_i}, \eeq where $S_N$ denotes the set of all the permutations of the integers $\{1,\hdots,N\}$, $\sgn (\sigma)$ returns $1$ if the permutation $\sigma$ is even and $-1$ if the permutation is odd and $A_{i,\sigma_i}$ denotes the element of the matrix $A$ in the $i^{\text{th}}$ row and the column defined by the $i^{\text{th}}$ element in the permutation $\sigma$.

nodes.name: Cofactor vector $V$ and the coefficients $k$, $n$
nodes.statement: We rewrite the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)$ as $\Phi(t+1|t)=\left[\Phi',\, W\varphi(t)+Zu(t|t)\right]$, where \begin{equation*} \Phi'=\left[ \ba{ccc} \Phi_{1,1} &\hdots & \Phi_{1,n_um-1}\\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ \Phi_{n_um,1}& \hdots & \Phi_{n_um,n_um-1} \ea \right], \end{equation*} with the elements $\Phi_{p,q}\in \bR,\,\, p=1,\hdots,n_um,\, q=1,\hdots,n_um-1$, denoting the corresponding elements of the applied regerssor vectors $\varphi(k),\, k=t-n_um+1,\hdots, t-1$. In addition, we denote by $S_{n_um}^i,\, i=1,\hdots, n_um$ the set of all the permutations of the integers $\{1,\hdots,n_um\}$ that have $n_um$ at the $i^{\text{th}}$ position. Based on this we define the vector $V \in \bR^{n_um}$ as: \beq V=\left[ \ba{c} \sum \limits_{\sigma \in S_{n_um}^1} sgn(\sigma) \prod\limits_{i=2}^{n_um}\Phi_{i,\sigma_i}\\ \sum \limits_{\sigma \in S_{n_um}^2} sgn(\sigma) \prod\limits_{i=1,\,i\neq 2}^{n_um}\Phi_{i,\sigma_i}\\ \vdots \\\sum \limits_{\sigma \in S_{n_um}^{n_um}} sgn(\sigma) \prod\limits_{ i=1,\, i\neq n_um}^{n_um}\Phi_{i,\sigma_i}\ea \right]. \eeq Then we can express $k$ and $n$ by using $V$ as: \beq \begin{aligned} k^T&=V^TZ\\ n&=V^TW\varphi(t). \end{aligned} \eeq
nodes.statement_short: $V$ collects the cofactors of the last column of $\Phi(t+1|t)$, giving $k^T=V^TZ$ and $n=V^TW\varphi(t)$.
nodes.genus: vector of signed permutation sums (cofactors) of $\Phi'$
differentia: each entry sums $sgn(\sigma)\prod \Phi_{i,\sigma_i}$ over permutations with $n_um$ in position $i$
